ideas.title: Phaser Game Scaffolder
ideas.summary: Describe a 2D game concept in plain English and instantly get a runnable, well-commented Phaser.js starter template you can open in the browser and hack in minutes. Removes the blank-page barrier for game dev beginners.
ideas.description: A single-page React app where you type a brief description of your game idea (e.g., 'a top-down maze where a robot collects keys while avoiding lasers') and Claude generates a complete, annotated Phaser.js game file. The generator picks sensible defaults for canvas size, physics, player movement, collectibles, and scoring based on the concept, and wraps the output in a self-contained HTML file. A live preview renders in an iframe right on the page. Inline comments explain every Phaser API call so the output doubles as a tutorial. A second Claude call produces a 'Next Steps' panel suggesting specific customizations for movement, art, and sound. The entire tool runs in a weekend: React + Vite frontend making direct Claude API calls, no backend needed.
keyFeatures: Natural-language game description → working Phaser.js game in one click
Annotated code with comments explaining every Phaser API call
Downloadable single-file HTML that runs anywhere
AI-generated Next Steps panel for extending each game system
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, Claude API (claude-sonnet-5), Phaser.js (loaded in generated template via CDN)
ideas.whyInteresting: The blank-page problem stops more game dev beginners than any technical obstacle. A working, readable starting point removes the first barrier, and the inline comments turn generated code into a tutorial. Useful as a personal tool and easily extensible into a classroom scaffold for game design courses.
ideas.inspiredBy: JetBrains AI Debugging Assistant's in-context AI explanations; Andrej Karpathy's Nanochat (one cohesive learning repo); Pisan's game development courses at UW Bothell

ideas.title: Live Accessibility Explainer
ideas.summary: A one-click browser bookmarklet that overlays real-time WCAG accessibility violations on any live web page during a class demo, with Claude generating short, disability-context explanations of who each issue affects and why — turning abstract rules into memorable teaching moments.
ideas.description: Instructors click the bookmarklet to inject axe-core into the current tab, which scans for WCAG violations without navigating away. Each violation is annotated with a small colored badge (red = critical, orange = serious) positioned next to the offending element. Clicking a badge fires a Claude Haiku call that returns a two-sentence empathy-grounded explanation (e.g., 'A user relying on a screen reader hears nothing useful for this button, so they cannot submit the form'). A summary panel slides in from the right showing violation counts by category and severity. No backend required — axe-core and the Claude API call both run client-side, with the instructor's key stored in localStorage. The bookmarklet is generated by a one-page setup app where instructors paste their API key, choose verbosity level (concise vs. detailed), and copy the bookmarklet link.
keyFeatures: One-click bookmarklet — no browser extension install required
axe-core powered WCAG 2.2 violation detection on any page
Visual badge overlay on the live page without navigation
Severity summary panel with counts by category
ideas.techStack: Vanilla JS bookmarklet, axe-core (injected via CDN), Claude API (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 for low latency), React + Vite setup page
ideas.whyInteresting: Most accessibility training stays abstract and checkbox-driven. Seeing violations on a real page during a live demo, with Claude narrating the human impact in plain English, creates empathy-based understanding that sticks. The bookmarklet format means zero setup friction — instructors use it on any site in any class within 30 seconds of setup.
ideas.inspiredBy: axe DevTools browser extension; Pisan's interest in accessibility in web courses; ITiCSE 2025 literature on tools that make abstract CS concepts concrete for students

ideas.title: Collaborative Student Wiki
ideas.summary: Students build a fully collaborative course knowledge base with AI-powered semantic article linking, one-click MCQ quiz generation, and personal learning tracking. A full-stack capstone that teaches React, Supabase, vector embeddings, and meaningful Claude API integration.
ideas.description: Students implement a Wikipedia-style knowledge base for a CS course topic of their choice (data structures, OS internals, networking, etc.). The core feature set spans four sprint-sized layers: week 1 is CRUD article authoring with Supabase auth and revision history; week 2 adds Supabase Realtime for live presence indicators showing who else is editing; week 3 introduces pgvector embeddings so the app auto-suggests related articles as the student types and enables semantic full-text search; week 4 adds a 'Quiz Me' button that sends the article body to Claude and returns three MCQs with explanations instantly, plus a personal 'I know this / needs review' tracker. The finished product is immediately useful to the whole class, and future cohorts inherit a growing knowledge base — giving the assignment a legacy dimension that raises motivation. Rubric can be structured around each sprint layer, making partial credit straightforward to assign.
keyFeatures: Collaborative markdown article editor with full revision history
pgvector-powered semantic related-article suggestions in real time
One-click MCQ quiz generation per article via Claude API
Personal learning tracker (knows / needs review) stored in Supabase
Live presence indicators showing which editors are active in each article
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, Supabase (auth + realtime + pgvector), Claude API (claude-sonnet-5), Marked.js for markdown rendering
ideas.whyInteresting: Students build something the whole class uses immediately — a powerful motivator. The project touches every layer of a modern web stack (auth, realtime, vector search, LLM integration) and uses AI for a purpose students can explain and evaluate. Scalable from a two-week sprint to a semester-long capstone depending on feature scope.
ideas.inspiredBy: OpenKnowledge (open-source AI-first Obsidian/Notion alternative featured on Hacker News, 2026); Wikipedia-style collaborative learning; Pisan's interest in RAG and embedding-based tools for education

ideas.title: Rubric-Grounded LLM Feedback for Code Readability in CS1: Scaling a Pilot and Closing the Structural-Formatting Gap
ideas.summary: A small pilot found GPT-4 can generate rubric-aligned readability feedback on naming and commenting but consistently fails on structural formatting. This research scales the experiment to hundreds of real submissions, tests multiple LLMs with calibrated prompting, and measures whether augmented feedback reduces readability defects in subsequent student work.
ideas.description: Ouh et al. (ITiCSE 2025) showed that GPT-4 can generate code readability feedback aligned with rubric criteria for naming and commenting, but only one of five test submissions received correct structural formatting feedback — the dimension that matters most for professional code style and that static linters alone cannot explain. This research extends the pilot in three directions. First, it scales evaluation from 5 to 500+ archived submissions from Pisan's Jolly Feedback system (CSS 142/143), enabling statistically reliable, per-dimension comparison of multiple LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, open-weight models) with and without rubric-grounding prompts. Second, it tests whether a static analysis pre-pass (Clang-Tidy / Checkstyle) that flags structural violations before the LLM prompt closes the formatting gap — combining rule-based detection precision with LLM-generated pedagogical explanation. Third, Phase 2 tracks whether students who receive the augmented feedback on one submission show measurably fewer readability defects on their next, providing a first large-N causal estimate of code-style feedback efficacy. Phase 1 is entirely computational and requires no new IRB approval.

papers.title: Can GPT4 Generate Effective Feedback on Code Readability?
papers.authors: Eng Lieh Ouh, Kar Way Tan, Siaw Ling Lo, Benjamin Kok Siew Gan
papers.abstract: This study explored the potential of GPT4 to generate feedback on code readability for students enrolled in a CS1 Java course. We developed rubrics based on three readability criteria: naming, commenting, and formatting. Results were mixed: while some feedback messages closely aligned with the rubrics, offering valuable insights, others fell short in providing corrective guidance. GPT-4 was particularly weak on structural code quality — only one of five test submissions received correct indentation, blank-line, and white-space feedback.
papers.relevance: Establishes the direct baseline this research extends: a 5-submission pilot with promising but inconsistent results, with the sharpest failure on structural formatting. The three-rubric-dimension framing, mixed-results finding, and call for refined guidelines and better prompts define exactly the research gap this project addresses.

additionalRefs.title: The Effects of Structured LLM-Generated Feedback on Programming Assignment Performance
additionalRefs.relevance: Studies how the structure of LLM-generated feedback (immediate vs. delayed, specific vs. general) affects performance on subsequent programming assignments — directly informs how feedback conditions should be designed in Phase 2 to maximize learning-outcome signal.

additionalRefs.title: LLM-based Multimodal Feedback Produces Equivalent Learning and Better Student Perceptions than Educator Feedback
additionalRefs.relevance: Demonstrates that well-designed LLM feedback can match or exceed educator feedback in learning outcomes while significantly improving student satisfaction — sets the benchmark expectations for the learning-outcome measurement in Phase 2 and justifies the investment in prompt calibration.

additionalRefs.title: Identifying Students' Code Quality Defects in Large Code Bases
additionalRefs.authors: Anshul Shah, Thomas Rexin, Gonzalo Allen-Perez et al.
additionalRefs.relevance: Classifies real code quality defects introduced by upper-division CS students into a taxonomy including Poor Design, Poor Documentation, Poor Formatting, and Unused Code — provides a complementary defect vocabulary for categorizing readability issues beyond the three-criterion rubric and informs annotation schema for the Phase 1 evaluation dataset.

researchPlan.overview: The project extends a 5-submission GPT-4 pilot into a large-scale, multi-LLM comparison on hundreds of real Jolly Feedback submissions, then tests whether a static-analysis pre-pass closes the structural-formatting gap. Phase 1 is fully computational; Phase 2 deploys the best configuration to a live course section and measures before/after defect rates on subsequent submissions. The six-month arc runs from dataset curation through a submitted paper.

milestones.deliverable: Annotated bibliography + curated dataset of 500+ CSS 142/143 submissions with known grader scores

milestones.goal: Ground-truth rubric coding and inter-rater agreement study
milestones.deliverable: Coded dataset with per-submission readability ratings on all three dimensions (naming, commenting, formatting), Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.7

milestones.goal: Multi-LLM evaluation with rubric-grounding and static-analysis hybrid
milestones.deliverable: Accuracy tables by LLM × prompting strategy × rubric dimension; best configuration identified

milestones.goal: Error analysis and ablation study on the formatting gap
milestones.deliverable: Detailed failure taxonomy for formatting feedback; ablation showing contribution of static-analysis pre-pass

milestones.goal: Phase 2 live deployment in CSS 142 and before/after defect measurement
milestones.deliverable: Submission defect counts across two consecutive assignments; preliminary effect-size estimate
Submitted paper draft to SIGCSE TS 2027 or ITiCSE 2027

researchPlan.resources: Jolly Feedback submission logs from CSS 142/143 (existing data asset); Claude and OpenAI API access for multi-LLM evaluation; Clang-Tidy/Checkstyle for static pre-pass; one research assistant for ground-truth rubric coding; IRB approval for Phase 2 live deployment.

risks.risk: Archived submission logs may have insufficient metadata to reconstruct grader intent for ground-truth coding
risks.mitigation: Cross-reference logs with original assignment rubrics and grader comments stored in Canvas; manually recode a random sample to validate

risks.risk: LLMs may pattern-match rubric wording rather than actually detecting code quality issues, inflating accuracy scores
risks.mitigation: Test with held-out rubric variants (synonym substitutions) and adversarial examples (code with rubric-mentioned keywords but correct style) to probe generalization

risks.risk: Phase 2 live deployment effect size may be too small to detect with one course section
risks.mitigation: Scope Phase 1 to establish a robust signal, and design Phase 2 as a within-student pre/post measurement (same student, consecutive assignments) rather than between-group, maximizing statistical power
